content: In April 2009, a novel influenza A (H1N1) virus was identified as the cause of respiratory illness in two children in the United States during March and April of that year. This virus was also linked to outbreaks of respiratory illness in Mexico. Within weeks, the virus spread across communities in North America and was detected in various regions worldwide by May 2009. On June 11, 2009, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared a global pandemic, signifying widespread community-level transmission of the novel influenza A (H1N1) virus in multiple areas globally. Transmission of the virus continued in both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres after June 2009, with expectations of increased activity in the Northern Hemisphere during the fall and winter seasons. Unlike seasonal influenza, evidence suggests that severe cases of novel influenza A (H1N1) infection have been relatively rare among older individuals. The highest hospitalization rates have been observed in individuals under 65 years of age. The clinical presentation of novel influenza A (H1N1) infection is similar to that of seasonal influenza, necessitating specific diagnostic testing to differentiate between the two. Influenza vaccination remains the most effective strategy for preventing influenza and its complications. However, current seasonal influenza vaccines are unlikely to provide protection against the novel influenza A (H1N1) virus. Vaccines specifically targeting the novel virus are under development, with licensed vaccines expected to become available in the United States by mid-October 2009. Initial vaccine supplies may be insufficient to meet demand, prompting the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) to recommend prioritizing vaccination for groups at highest risk of infection or complications. The ACIP has identified five initial target groups for vaccination: pregnant women, individuals who live with or care for infants under six months of age, healthcare and emergency medical services personnel, children and young adults aged 6 months to 24 years, and individuals aged 25 to 64 years with medical conditions that increase their risk of influenza-related complications. If vaccine availability is limited, priority should be given to a subset of these groups. As vaccine supplies increase, vaccination efforts should expand to include additional groups. The ACIP will continue to review new epidemiologic and clinical data and may revise recommendations as needed. Human infections with the novel influenza A (H1N1) virus were first identified in April 2009, and cases have since been reported worldwide. Serologic studies indicate that a large majority of the population is susceptible to the virus, raising concerns about the potential for widespread infection. The novel virus is antigenically and genetically distinct from other human influenza A (H1N1) viruses that have circulated since 1977. As of August 1, 2009, circulating novel influenza A (H1N1) viruses appear to be antigenically similar. The clinical features of novel influenza A (H1N1) infection resemble those of seasonal influenza. Definitive diagnosis requires specific testing, such as real-time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) or viral culture. Rapid influenza diagnostic tests (RIDTs) may detect the novel virus but have limited sensitivity, estimated at 40%-70%. Negative RIDT results should not exclude the diagnosis of novel influenza A (H1N1) infection. The age distribution of confirmed cases, severity of illness, and prevalence of medical risk factors among severely ill individuals have been consistent across countries and over time. In the United States, as of July 31, 2009, the median age of individuals with laboratory-confirmed infections was 12 years, with the highest infection incidence among those aged 5-24 years. The lowest incidence was observed among individuals aged 65 years and older. Similar findings have been reported in other countries. Hospitalization data reveal a striking difference in age distribution compared to seasonal influenza. As of July 31, 2009, the median age of hospitalized individuals with laboratory-confirmed novel influenza A (H1N1) infection was 20 years, with the highest hospitalization rates among young children and individuals under 65 years of age. In contrast, seasonal influenza typically results in the highest hospitalization and mortality rates among individuals aged 65 years and older. As of July 31, 2009, only 5% of hospitalizations and 8% of reported deaths attributed to novel influenza A (H1N1) infection occurred among individuals aged 65 years and older. Certain medical risk factors for severe infection, such as chronic heart, lung, renal, or liver disease, cancer, immunosuppression, and pregnancy, are similar to those identified in studies of seasonal influenza. Pregnant women have been disproportionately affected, with hospitalization rates four times higher than the general population. Obesity, particularly morbid obesity, has been noted among hospitalized patients, although most of these individuals had other medical risk factors. Investigations are ongoing to determine whether obesity is an independent risk factor for severe infection. The epidemiology of novel influenza A (H1N1) infection is still under investigation, and characteristics may evolve as transmission continues. Schools, colleges, and camps have been frequent sources of community transmission. During spring and summer 2009, many schools and camps in the United States were temporarily dismissed due to outbreak concerns, causing significant community impact. Laboratory-confirmed cases likely underestimate the true incidence of influenza illness caused by the novel virus, as testing has focused on individuals with more severe infections. Community surveys have identified self-reported influenza-like illness (ILI) among approximately 6% of surveyed populations in areas with focal outbreaks. Transmission of the novel virus in healthcare settings has been reported, with some cases of probable patient-to-healthcare personnel transmission. Among healthcare personnel with available information on personal protective equipment use, only a minority reported consistent use of surgical masks or N95 respirators. Community-acquired infections among healthcare personnel raise concerns about the potential introduction of the virus into healthcare settings. Vaccines against the novel influenza A (H1N1) virus are being produced using methods similar to those for seasonal influenza vaccines. Both live attenuated and inactivated monovalent vaccine formulations will be available initially, and neither will contain adjuvants. The FDA and WHO have selected the A/California/07/2009 (H1N1) strain for use in vaccine production. In previously unvaccinated individuals, two doses of the vaccine may be required to achieve protection. Ongoing studies will provide additional information about immune responses and dosing requirements. The ACIP recommends that initial vaccination efforts focus on five target groups at higher risk for influenza or complications, those likely to encounter the virus in occupational settings, or close contacts of infants under six months of age. If vaccine availability is limited, priority should be given to a subset of these groups. As vaccine supplies increase, vaccination should expand to include all members of the initial target groups and eventually other adult populations. Decisions about expanding vaccination efforts should be made at the local level based on vaccine availability and demand. The CDC and other public health agencies will monitor vaccine supply and inform the public of any delays or shortages.
